summary: Explains problems with the DIGEST-MD5 SASL authentication mechanism from RFC 2831, marks it obsolete in the IANA SASL registry, and moves RFC 2831 to Historic status.

plainLanguage.summary: DIGEST-MD5 was a way to prove your password without sending it, but it had too many problems. This note retires it and tells people to stop using it.

questions: why was digest-md5 moved to historic
subtitle: Why the DIGEST-MD5 login mechanism was declared obsolete and RFC 2831 moved to Historic.

tldr.problem: DIGEST-MD5, a SASL login mechanism defined in RFC 2831, turned out to be too complex to implement fully and securely, and its cryptography had aged badly.
tldr.mechanism: This memo lists the mechanism's problems, concludes that fixing them is not worth the cost, marks DIGEST-MD5 as OBSOLETE in the IANA SASL registry and moves RFC 2831 to Historic.
tldr.outcome: DIGEST-MD5 is deprecated in favor of newer password-based mechanisms such as the SCRAM family.

facts.label: IANA change
facts.value: DIGEST-MD5 marked OBSOLETE in the SASL registry

today: RFC 6331 is an Informational RFC that obsoletes RFC 2831, the DIGEST-MD5 specification, and moves it to Historic. No later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating RFC 6331.

sections.title: What DIGEST-MD5 Was
sections.content:
RFC 2831 defined how HTTP Digest Authentication can serve as a SASL (Simple Authentication and Security Layer) mechanism for any protocol with a SASL profile. It was meant as an improvement over CRAM-MD5 and as a convenient single mechanism for web, email, LDAP and other protocols.

Many implementors reported that its extra complexity makes it difficult to implement fully and securely. RFC 6331 collects an incomplete list of problems and then retires the mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: DIGEST-MD5 was a way for programs to prove who they are to a server. It was meant to be handy for everything, but it turned out to be hard to build correctly.

sections.title: Complexity and Interoperability Problems
sections.content:
The mechanism has too many options and modes, some poorly described and rarely implemented. The qop directive may hold several values, and several qop directives may appear, but handling is unspecified: some implementations merge them, others treat it as an error. The document is also unclear on whether an empty authorization identity must be omitted or may be sent with an empty value.

Compatibility with HTTP Digest forces down-conversion of usernames and passwords from UTF-8 to ISO-8859-1 when they fit, and the handling of quoted strings and escaping is not properly described. The document uses the ABNF of RFC 822, with implied folding whitespace, which many implementations do not accept.

It also uses "realms" without saying how they should be named or entered in user interfaces, so many clients have confusing realm handling. Storing an inner hash of username, realm and password is rarely done, since it is not compatible with widely deployed Unix password databases and changing the username would invalidate it.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules had so many options and unclear parts that different programs understood them differently, so they sometimes could not talk to each other.

sections.title: Security and Cryptography Problems
sections.content:
The descriptions of the DES/3DES and RC4 security layers are inadequate for independently developed interoperable implementations. The outer hash, the response directive, does not protect the whole exchange, so the mechanism is open to man-in-the-middle attacks such as modifying the list of supported qops or ciphers.

Missing features include channel bindings, hash agility (no easy way to replace MD5), and SASLprep or any other Unicode normalization of usernames and passwords.

The primitives are dated too. MD5 is weak enough that a brute force attack is easy with common hardware (RFC 6151). RC4 is prone to attack as a security layer unless the initial key stream is discarded (RFC 6229), and DES is considered insecure because of its small key space (RFC 3766). The memo notes that most of these problems are already present in HTTP Digest.
sections.plainLanguage: The lock was easy to pick, and an attacker standing in the middle could meddle with the settings the two sides agreed on. The ingredients were also old and weak.

sections.title: The Decision and IANA Action
sections.content:
DIGEST-MD5 could in principle be fixed because it is extensible, but that would add complexity to an already complex mechanism. A "fixed" version would likely either not interoperate with existing RFC 2831 implementations or be vulnerable to downgrade attacks, so the effort is not worth the cost.

The memo accepts that DIGEST-MD5 has seen some deployment, but says that as implemented it is not a reasonable candidate for further standardization. IANA changed the "Intended usage" of the DIGEST-MD5 entry in the SASL mechanism registry to OBSOLETE.
sections.plainLanguage: Patching it would make an already messy machine even messier, so the authors decided it was better to retire it and replace it.

sections.title: What to Use Instead
sections.content:
The memo says DIGEST-MD5 should be deprecated in favor of one or more new password-based mechanisms then being designed. The Salted Challenge Response Authentication Mechanism (SCRAM) family of SASL mechanisms, defined in RFC 5802, was developed to provide similar features with a better design.

The Security Considerations section says only that security issues are discussed throughout the document.
sections.plainLanguage: A newer, better handshake called SCRAM was built to do the same job without the old problems.
